_method: primary sources fetched live (gov.uk statutory code of practice, HM Treasury multiplier-effects doc, gov.uk ERA timeline update of 7 Aug 2026, HMRC VAT brief 5/2026). Scopes corrected at assembly: Tips Act and ERA measures extend to England+Wales+Scotland only (not NI) — scope level 'nations', added to the matcher for exactly this. Scotland/Wales business rates and NI tips law excluded as unverified.

entries.title: Employment (Allocation of Tips) Act 2023 — fair allocation, policy, records, payment deadline
entries.fact: Since 1 October 2024, employers in Great Britain must pass on 100% of qualifying tips fairly, keep a written tipping policy and a 3-year tipping record, and pay tips out no later than the end of the month after the month the customer paid them.

source.quote: employers must ensure that all tips are distributed to staff, at the latest, by the end of the month following the month in which the tips are paid by customers

entries.angle: For a multi-site group, the Tips Act's per-site written policy, per-worker allocation records and month-following payment deadline (in force since Oct 2024) turn tronc admin into a recurring payroll-adjacent workload at every location — a concrete, dated hook about admin time rather than a scare line.
entries.proof_pairing: Customer proof about payroll/tronc admin time saved per site, or accurate per-shift labour and payroll data reducing back-office hours.
entries.caveats: The Act extends to England, Wales and Scotland only (sections marked E+W+S; no NI extent) — scope enforces this. Tips-heavy relevance: strongest for table-service (FSR), weaker for QSR. Facts only — never advise on tronc structuring.

entries.title: England 2026 revaluation + permanent lower RHL multipliers (38.2p / 43p) from 1 April 2026
entries.fact: From 1 April 2026 the 2026 revaluation took effect in England alongside permanently lower retail/hospitality/leisure multipliers — 38.2p (RV under £51,000) and 43p (RV £51,000–£499,999), both 5p below the national equivalents — funded by a 50.8p high-value multiplier on all properties with RV £500,000 or above.
entries._quantification_rejected: HM Treasury's factsheet gives £900m/year across 750,000+ RHL properties (≈£1,200 average per property) — deliberately NOT used as a per_site_per_year quantification: it is a sector average, and a given site's bill can have risen with its new 2026 rateable value, so scaling the average by the account's site count would present a number that is not theirs (violates the quantify-on-their-footprint rule). Context only.

source.quote: Table 2.A 2026-27 multipliers ... Small business RHL multiplier 38.2p RHL hereditaments with RVs under £51,000; Standard RHL multiplier 43p RHL hereditaments with RVs between £51,000 and £499,999 ... High-value multiplier 50.8p All hereditaments with RVs of £500,000 or above ... The next revaluation will take effect from 1 April 2026 ... As business rates are a devolved tax, these policies, and the effects outlined in this document, apply to England only.

entries.angle: Since 1 April 2026 every English site's rates bill moved twice at once — new rateable value plus the new permanent RHL multipliers — so a group's per-site occupancy costs just re-based; a dated opener can reference how finance teams are reconciling the new bills across the estate.
entries.proof_pairing: Customer proof on per-site P&L visibility / prime-cost tracking across locations, so site-level cost changes are caught in-month.
entries.caveats: England only — business rates are devolved; do not use for Scotland, Wales or NI sites (their schemes were not verified this session). Net effect per site depends on the new RV: a site or HQ with RV ≥ £500,000 pays the higher 50.8p multiplier. Supporting context only (quantification deliberately withheld — see _quantification_rejected): if the £1,200 average is ever mentioned in copy it must be framed as 'an average across RHL properties', never as the prospect's saving. No advice on rates appeals.

entries.title: Employment Rights Act 2025: unfair dismissal qualifying period cut to 6 months from 1 January 2027
entries.fact: Under the government's updated Employment Rights Act 2025 timeline (updated 7 August 2026), the unfair dismissal qualifying period is reduced to 6 months for dismissals from 1 January 2027, with compensatory awards uncapped — a revision from the originally proposed day-one right.

source.quote: reduction of unfair dismissal qualifying period to 6 months, for dismissals from 1 January 2027, and uncapping compensatory awards

entries.angle: From 1 January 2027, dismissals of staff past 6 months' service carry unfair-dismissal exposure in a sector with high early-tenure churn — a dated hook about how groups are tightening documentation of hours, performance and probation across sites before the deadline.
entries.proof_pairing: Customer proof on clean, auditable scheduling/timekeeping and HR records per site; onboarding-to-rota data hygiene.
entries.caveats: Great Britain scope (NI employment law is devolved — not verified this session; scope enforces GB). It is a 6-month qualifying period, NOT a day-one right — the original day-one proposal was revised; never say 'day-one'. Facts and dates only, no advice on dismissal or contract practice.

entries.title: Employment Rights Act 2025: right to guaranteed hours for zero/low-hours workers — 2027, timings TBC
entries.fact: The government's Employment Rights Act 2025 timeline (updated 7 August 2026) lists the right to guaranteed hours, plus rights to reasonable notice of shifts and short-notice payments, under measures taking effect in 2027, with timings to be updated after consultation.

source.quote: introduction of the right to guaranteed hours and the right to reasonable notice and short notice payments (timings will be updated after consultation)

entries.angle: Guaranteed-hours and shift-notice rights are on the government's 2027 timeline, which means 2026 rota data becomes the baseline operators will be measured against — a dated opener on how multi-site groups are getting scheduling and hours data in order ahead of consultation outcomes.
entries.proof_pairing: Customer proof on demand-based scheduling accuracy, rota stability, and hours-worked reporting per site.
entries.caveats: effective_date 2027-12-31 is a placeholder for 'during 2027' — exact commencement is explicitly TBC after consultation; always say '2027, timings to be confirmed', never a specific date. Status is proposed-with-year, not firmly scheduled. GB scope; NI not verified. No advice on contract redesign.

entries.title: Temporary 5% VAT on children's meals and family attractions, 25 June – 1 September 2026
entries.fact: A legislated temporary 5% reduced VAT rate (SI 2026/576) applies from 25 June to 1 September 2026 inclusive to children's meals sold for consumption on the premises of restaurants, cafés and similar establishments, and to qualifying child/family admissions to attractions.

source.quote: The reduced rate applies from 25 June 2026 to 1 September 2026 (inclusive). ... The reduced rate applies to the supply of children's meals where both of the following conditions are met: the meal is held out for sale only as a meal for children [and] the meal is supplied as part of catering services by a restaurant, café or similar establishment for consumption on the premises.

entries.angle: The 5% VAT window on eat-in children's meals ends 1 September 2026, so finance teams at family-dining groups are mid-way through a rate switch on part of the menu — a dated, specific hook about handling split VAT treatment across sites and tills.
entries.proof_pairing: Customer proof on menu/EPOS data accuracy and finance close speed across sites.
entries.caveats: Narrow scope: eat-in children's meals and qualifying family/child admissions only — takeaway meals excluded; the general 20% rate on other hospitality supplies is unchanged. EXPIRES 1 September 2026 (review_by enforces this) — do not use after that date without re-verification. Not evidence of any broader hospitality VAT cut.
